title: Giving and receiving feedback at work

lessons.title: Ask for feedback on your work
lessons.goal: I can ask for feedback on my work.

newItems.definition: Comments about what someone did, to help them do better.
newItems.example: My manager gave me useful feedback on my report.

newItems.definition: Clear and exact, about one thing only.
newItems.example: Please give me specific examples, not general comments.

newItems.definition: To share comments about someone's work.
newItems.example: My manager gives feedback every Friday.

newItems.definition: Used to ask if someone has thought about an idea.
newItems.example: Have you considered a shorter meeting?

newItems.definition: Used to suggest something that could be useful.
newItems.example: It might help to ask the team first.

mainWord.definition: Comments about what someone did, to help them do better.
mainWord.example: My manager gave me useful feedback on my report.

lessons.mainWordForms: Feedback is a noun. Feedback has no plural. Feedback is comments about what someone did, to help them do better. My manager gave me useful feedback on my report.
lessons.expression: Could you give me some feedback on my report?
lessons.use: Use this when you want someone to tell you what they think of your work.
lessons.expressionTask: Daniel finishes his first report at work. What does he ask Maya?
lessons.grammar: Asking for opinions: Could you give me some feedback on + noun?
lessons.pattern: Could you give me some feedback on my report?
lessons.task: Could you give me some ___ on my report?
lessons.example: Could you give me some feedback on my report?
context: Daniel finishes his first report at work. He wants Maya's opinion.
Could you give me some feedback on my report?
dialogue: Daniel: Good morning, Maya. I finished my first report. Could you give me some feedback on my report?
Maya: Of course, Daniel. I will read it this morning. Do you want specific comments?
Daniel: Yes, please. Specific comments help me a lot.
Maya: Good. Have you considered a shorter title? It might help to keep the title short.
Daniel: That is a good idea. I will change the title today.
Maya: Good. I will give feedback on the report this afternoon.
lessons.listening: On Monday, Daniel finishes his report at the office. He asks his team lead, Maya, for help. He says, 'Could you give me some feedback on my report?' Maya says, 'Of course. I will read it this morning. Do you want specific comments?' Daniel says, 'Yes, please. Specific comments help me a lot.' Maya says she will give feedback on the report in the afternoon.
lessons.question: Who does Daniel ask for feedback?
lessons.reading: Daniel is new at work. On Monday, he finishes his first report, and he wants to know what his team thinks of it. He goes to his team lead, Maya, and says, 'Could you give me some feedback on my report?' Maya says, 'Of course. I will read it this morning.' Daniel says, 'Please give me specific comments. I want to learn.' Maya reads the report after lunch. She likes the ideas, but the title is very long. She says, 'Have you considered a shorter title? It might help to keep the title short and clear.' Daniel says, 'That is a good idea. I will change it today.' In the afternoon, Maya gives feedback on the report. She says the first part is clear and the last part is strong. Daniel is happy. He says, 'Thank you, Maya. Your feedback helps me a lot. Now I know what to do next.'
lessons.readingQ: What does Daniel ask Maya to do?
lessons.readingA: He asks her to give him feedback on his first report.
lessons.speaking: Tell a friend about a time you asked someone for feedback. What did you ask? What did they say? How did it help you?
lessons.speakingSample: I asked my manager for feedback on my first report. I said, 'Could you give me some feedback on my report?' She read it in the morning and gave me specific comments in the afternoon. She said, 'Have you considered a shorter title? It might help to keep the title short.' I changed the title that day. Her feedback helped me a lot.
lessons.writing: Write a short email to a colleague. Ask for feedback on a report. Say what you want them to look at.
lessons.writingSample: Dear Priya, I have finished my first report, and I would like your opinion. Could you give me some feedback on my report? Please give me specific comments. I want to know if my ideas are clear and if my title is good. Have you considered the last part? It might help to read the last part first. I will change the report after your feedback. Thank you for your help. I am happy to learn from you. Best, Daniel
lessons.sound: Feedback has its strongest beat on FEED. In feedback, say BACK clearly at the end. In specific, say CIF clearly in the middle.
lessons.model: My manager gave me useful feedback on my report.
lessons.wordTask: Who gave Daniel feedback on his first report?
lessons.wordSample: Maya, his team lead, gave Daniel feedback on his first report.

lessons.title: Give constructive feedback to a colleague
lessons.goal: I can give constructive feedback to a colleague.

newItems.definition: Helpful, and made to improve something, not just to criticize.
newItems.example: She gave me constructive advice about my presentation.

newItems.definition: Comments that say what is wrong with something.
newItems.example: He took the criticism calmly and asked how to improve.

newItems.definition: Used to give a gentle suggestion.
newItems.example: One thing I'd suggest is to start earlier.

newItems.definition: Used to say what you really think.
newItems.example: To be honest, I did not like the first plan.

newItems.word: let me put it this way
newItems.definition: Used to explain something in a different way.
newItems.example: Let me put it this way: the cost is too high.

mainWord.definition: Helpful, and made to improve something, not just to criticize.
mainWord.example: She gave me constructive advice about my presentation.

lessons.mainWordForms: Constructive is an adjective. Constructive feedback is helpful, and it is made to improve something, not just to criticize. She gave me constructive advice about my presentation.
lessons.expression: One thing I'd suggest is to start with a short summary.
lessons.use: Use this when you want to give a gentle suggestion.
lessons.expressionTask: Priya wants to give Daniel feedback. What does Maya suggest she say first?
lessons.grammar: Giving suggestions: It might be better to + verb
lessons.pattern: It might be better to start with a short summary.
lessons.task: It might be better to ___ with a short summary.
lessons.example: It might be better to start with a short summary.
context: Priya asks Maya how to give feedback to Daniel.
One thing I'd suggest is to start with a short summary.
dialogue: Priya: Maya, Daniel asked me for feedback on his report. How can I give constructive feedback?
Maya: Start with the good parts. Then talk about the parts that need work.
Priya: What if my criticism is hard to hear?
Maya: Be kind and clear. One thing I'd suggest is to start with a short summary.
Priya: To be honest, the ending is too long. Let me put it this way: the first part is clear, but the last part is hard to follow.
Maya: That is good. Daniel will listen to constructive feedback like that.
lessons.listening: On Tuesday, Priya reads Daniel's report. Daniel asked her for feedback, and she wants to give constructive feedback. She starts with the good parts. She says, 'Your first part is clear.' Then she talks about the ending. She says, 'One thing I'd suggest is to start with a short summary.' Daniel listens and says, 'Thank you, Priya. That helps me a lot.'
lessons.question: What does Priya say first about the report?
lessons.reading: On Tuesday, Priya reads Daniel's report. Daniel asked her for feedback, and she wants to give constructive feedback. She knows that good feedback starts with the good parts. First, she says, 'Your first part is clear, and your ideas are easy to follow.' Then she talks about the ending. She says, 'To be honest, the ending is too long. Let me put it this way: the first part is clear, but the last part is hard to follow.' Priya is a little afraid. She does not want her criticism to hurt Daniel. Maya says, 'Do not be afraid. One thing I'd suggest is to start with a short summary. Then talk about the problem in a kind way.' Priya follows Maya's advice. Daniel listens to her and says, 'Thank you, Priya. Your feedback is clear, and I know what to do next.' Priya is happy. She gave constructive feedback, and Daniel is glad to hear it.
lessons.readingQ: How does Priya give feedback to Daniel?
lessons.readingA: She starts with the good parts, then talks about the ending in a kind way.
lessons.speaking: Tell a friend how you give feedback to a colleague. What do you say first? How do you talk about a problem?
lessons.speakingSample: When I give feedback to a colleague, I start with the good parts. Then I talk about the problem. I say, 'To be honest, the ending is too long. Let me put it this way: the first part is clear, but the last part is hard to follow.' I do not want my criticism to hurt my colleague. One thing I'd suggest is a short summary.
lessons.writing: Write a short email to a colleague. Give feedback on their report. Start with the good parts, then talk about one problem.
lessons.writingSample: Dear Daniel, Thank you for your report. I read it this morning, and I want to give you some feedback. Your first part is clear, and your ideas are easy to follow. To be honest, the ending is too long. Let me put it this way: the first part is clear, but the last part is hard to follow. One thing I'd suggest is to start with a short summary. Then the report will be easy to read. I am glad to work with you. Best, Priya
lessons.sound: Constructive has its strongest beat on STRUC. In constructive, say TIVE clearly at the end. In criticism, say CRIT clearly at the start.
lessons.model: She gave me constructive advice about my presentation.
lessons.wordTask: What does Priya say first to Daniel?
lessons.wordSample: She says his first part is clear and his ideas are easy to follow.

lessons.title: Respond to criticism without getting defensive
lessons.goal: I can respond to criticism without getting defensive.

newItems.definition: Trying to protect yourself from criticism, often too quickly.
newItems.example: Try not to sound defensive when someone points out a mistake.

newItems.definition: To accept that something is true or exists.
newItems.example: She acknowledged her mistake and apologized.

newItems.definition: Used to say you understand someone.
newItems.example: I see what you mean. The plan is too long.

newItems.definition: Used to agree that someone's idea is reasonable.
newItems.example: That's a fair point. Let us change the time.

newItems.definition: Used to thank someone for showing a problem.
newItems.example: Thanks for pointing that out. I will fix it.

mainWord.definition: Trying to protect yourself from criticism, often too quickly.
mainWord.example: Try not to sound defensive when someone points out a mistake.

lessons.mainWordForms: Defensive is an adjective. To be defensive is to try to protect yourself from criticism, often too quickly. Try not to sound defensive when someone points out a mistake.
lessons.use: Use this when someone shows you a problem and you want to thank them.
lessons.expressionTask: Daniel hears criticism about his report. What does he say to Priya?
lessons.grammar: Responding to criticism: Thank you for + verb-ing
lessons.pattern: Thank you for pointing that out.
lessons.example: Thank you for pointing that out.
context: Priya gives Daniel feedback about the ending of his report.
dialogue: Priya: Daniel, your first part is clear, but the ending is too long.
Daniel: I see what you mean. The last part is hard to follow.
Priya: Yes. It is a fair point, I think. The report will be better with a short ending.
Daniel: That's a fair point. I will make the ending shorter today.
Priya: Good. I am glad you are not defensive. You listen well.
Daniel: Thanks for pointing that out. I acknowledge the problem, and I will fix it.
lessons.listening: On Wednesday, Priya talks to Daniel about his report. She says the ending is too long. Daniel does not get angry. He says, 'I see what you mean. The last part is hard to follow.' Priya says she is glad he listens well. Daniel says, 'That's a fair point. Thanks for pointing that out. I will make the ending shorter today.'
lessons.question: How does Daniel respond to Priya's criticism?
lessons.reading: On Wednesday, Priya talks to Daniel about his report. She says the ending is too long and hard to follow. Daniel takes a deep breath. He does not want to sound defensive. He says, 'I see what you mean. The last part is hard to follow.' Priya says, 'I am glad you listen well. Many people get angry when they hear criticism.' Daniel says, 'That's a fair point. I acknowledge the problem, and I will fix it today.' He makes the ending shorter. In the afternoon, he shows the new ending to Priya. She reads it and says, 'This is much better. The report is clear now.' Daniel says, 'Thanks for pointing that out. Your feedback helped me a lot.' Maya hears them and says, 'Good work. Daniel, you listened well. Priya, your feedback was kind and clear.'
lessons.readingQ: What does Daniel do when Priya talks about the ending?
lessons.readingA: He listens, acknowledges the problem, and fixes it the same day.
lessons.speaking: Tell a friend about a time someone criticized your work. How did you respond? What did you say? What did you do next?
lessons.speakingSample: Last week, my colleague said my report was too long. I took a deep breath. I said, 'I see what you mean. The last part is hard to follow.' I said, 'That's a fair point. I acknowledge the problem, and I will fix it today.' I made the ending shorter. Then I said, 'Thanks for pointing that out.' I did not sound defensive, and my colleague was glad.
lessons.writing: Write a short email to a colleague. Thank them for their feedback. Say what you will change.
lessons.writingSample: Dear Priya, Thank you for your feedback on my report. You said the ending was too long, and you were right. I see what you mean. The last part was hard to follow. I acknowledge the problem, and I will fix it today. I will make the ending shorter and clearer. Thanks for pointing that out. Your feedback helped me a lot. I did not feel defensive, because your words were kind and clear. I will show you the new ending in the afternoon. Best, Daniel
lessons.sound: Defensive has its strongest beat on FEN. In defensive, say SIVE clearly at the end. In acknowledge, say NOWL clearly in the middle.
lessons.model: Try not to sound defensive when someone points out a mistake.
lessons.wordTask: What does Daniel say when Priya talks about the ending?
lessons.wordSample: He says, 'I see what you mean. The last part is hard to follow.'

lessons.title: Praise good work in specific detail
lessons.goal: I can praise good work in specific detail.

newItems.definition: Extremely good; better than most.
newItems.example: His outstanding work won the team an award.

newItems.definition: Unusual and worth noticing.
newItems.example: She made remarkable progress in six months.

newItems.definition: Very useful or worth a lot.
newItems.example: Your advice is very valuable to me.

newItems.definition: Used to praise someone for something they did.
newItems.example: Well done on your presentation!

newItems.definition: Used to praise someone and ask them to continue.
newItems.example: Your report was excellent. Keep up the good work!

mainWord.example: His outstanding work won the team an award.

lessons.mainWordForms: Outstanding is an adjective. Outstanding work is extremely good, better than most. His outstanding work won the team an award.
lessons.use: Use this to praise someone for something they did well.
lessons.expressionTask: Daniel gives a presentation to the team. What does Maya say to him?
lessons.grammar: Present perfect for achievements: have or has + past participle
lessons.pattern: Daniel has done outstanding work this week.
lessons.task: Daniel has ___ outstanding work this week.
lessons.example: Daniel has done outstanding work this week.
context: Daniel gives a presentation to the team on Thursday.
dialogue: Maya: Daniel, your presentation was excellent. Well done on your presentation!
Daniel: Thank you, Maya. I worked hard on it all week.
Maya: Your work was outstanding. The first part was clear and strong.
Priya: Yes. Your ideas were remarkable. I learned a lot from you.
Daniel: Thank you both. Your feedback helped me a lot.
Maya: Keep up the good work, Daniel. Your help is valuable to the team.
lessons.listening: On Thursday morning, Daniel gives a presentation to the team. He talks about his report and his new ending. Maya listens and says, 'Well done on your presentation! Your work was outstanding.' Priya says, 'Your ideas were remarkable. I learned a lot from you.' Daniel says, 'Thank you both. Your feedback helped me a lot.'
lessons.question: What does Maya say about Daniel's work?
lessons.reading: On Thursday morning, Daniel gives a presentation to the team. He talks about his report and his new ending. He speaks clearly, and his ideas are easy to follow. When he finishes, Maya says, 'Well done on your presentation! Your work was outstanding.' Priya says, 'Your ideas were remarkable. I learned a lot from you.' Daniel smiles. He worked hard all week, and now his team is happy with his work. Maya says, 'Daniel, your help is valuable to the team. You listen well, and you learn fast. Keep up the good work!' Daniel says, 'Thank you both. Your feedback helped me a lot. I asked for help, I listened, and I made my work better.' Maya says, 'That is the way to learn. Good work is not luck. It is clear ideas, hard work, and good feedback.'
lessons.readingQ: What does Maya say to Daniel after his presentation?
lessons.readingA: She says his work was outstanding and tells him to keep up the good work.
lessons.speaking: Tell a friend about a time someone praised your work. What did they say? How did you feel? What did you do next?
lessons.speakingSample: Last week, I gave a presentation to my team. When I finished, my manager said, 'Well done on your presentation! Your work was outstanding.' My colleague said, 'Your ideas were remarkable. I learned a lot from you.' My manager said, 'Your help is valuable to the team. Keep up the good work!' I thanked them both. Their words gave me new energy for my next report.
lessons.writing: Write a short email to a colleague. Praise their work in specific detail. Say what was good and why it helped the team.
lessons.writingSample: Dear Priya, I want to thank you for your help with my report. Well done on your presentation on Thursday! Your ideas were remarkable, and I learned a lot from you. Your work was outstanding. The first part was clear, and the last part was strong. Your help is valuable to the team. You listen well, and you explain ideas in a clear way. Keep up the good work! I am glad to work with you, and I hope we can work together again soon. Best, Daniel
lessons.sound: Outstanding has its strongest beat on STAND. In outstanding, say ING clearly at the end. In remarkable, say MARK clearly at the start.
lessons.model: His outstanding work won the team an award.
lessons.wordTask: What does Maya say about Daniel's presentation?
lessons.wordSample: She says, 'Well done on your presentation! Your work was outstanding.'

lessons.title: Suggest improvements diplomatically

newItems.definition: Careful not to upset people when you say something difficult.
newItems.example: A tactful manager gives bad news kindly.

newItems.definition: Honest and direct, even if it is hard to hear.
newItems.example: I want your candid opinion, not polite praise.

newItems.definition: A change that makes something better.
newItems.example: There has been a big improvement in his writing.

newItems.definition: A chance to do something better.
newItems.example: The report is good, but there is room for improvement.

newItems.definition: The parts of your work that could be better.
newItems.example: Let us talk about areas to improve on.

mainWord.definition: Careful not to upset people when you say something difficult.
mainWord.example: A tactful manager gives bad news kindly.

lessons.mainWordForms: Tactful is an adjective. A tactful person is careful not to upset people when they say something difficult. A tactful manager gives bad news kindly.
lessons.expression: Perhaps you could make the ending shorter.
lessons.use: Use this to suggest a change in a polite way.
lessons.expressionTask: Priya wants Daniel to change his report. How does she say it politely?
lessons.grammar: Diplomatic language: Perhaps you could + verb
lessons.pattern: Perhaps you could make the ending shorter.
lessons.task: Perhaps you could ___ the ending shorter.
lessons.example: Perhaps you could make the ending shorter.
context: Priya talks to Daniel about his report on Friday.
Perhaps you could make the ending shorter.
dialogue: Priya: Daniel, your report is good. Can I share a candid thought?
Daniel: Of course, Priya. I want to hear what you really think.
Priya: Perhaps you could make the ending shorter. The ideas are good, but the last part is long.
Daniel: Thank you. I will make it shorter today.
Priya: You are a good listener. A tactful word can help a lot.
Daniel: Yes. There is always room for improvement, and I want to learn.
lessons.listening: On Friday, Priya talks to Daniel about his report. She has a candid thought, and she wants to be tactful. She says, 'Perhaps you could make the ending shorter.' Daniel says, 'Thank you. I will make it shorter today.' Priya says, 'There is always room for improvement.' Daniel says he wants to learn more every week.
lessons.question: How does Priya suggest the change?
lessons.correct: Perhaps you could make the ending shorter
lessons.other: You must change the ending now
lessons.reading: On Friday, Priya talks to Daniel about his report. She has a candid thought: the ending is still a little long. She wants to be tactful, so she says, 'Perhaps you could make the ending shorter. The ideas are good, but the last part is long.' Daniel says, 'Thank you. I will make it shorter today.' Priya is glad. She says, 'There is always room for improvement. We can talk about areas to improve on every week.' Daniel says, 'Yes. I want to learn. What is one improvement I can make this week?' Priya says, 'Your first part is clear. Keep the first part, and make the last part short. That is one improvement.' Daniel makes the change in the afternoon. He shows the new ending to Priya. She reads it and says, 'This is much better. Your report is clear now.' Daniel says, 'Thank you. A tactful word can help a lot.'
lessons.readingQ: What does Priya suggest to Daniel?
lessons.readingA: She suggests he make the ending shorter.
lessons.speaking: Tell a friend how you suggest a change to a colleague. What do you say? How do you stay polite? What did they do?
lessons.speakingSample: When I want a colleague to change something, I try to be tactful. I say, 'Perhaps you could make the ending shorter. The ideas are good, but the last part is long.' I say, 'There is always room for improvement. We can talk about areas to improve on every week.' My colleague listens and makes the change. A tactful word can help a lot.
lessons.writing: Write a short email to a colleague. Suggest one improvement to their report. Be polite and clear.
lessons.writingSample: Dear Daniel, Thank you for your report. It is clear and easy to follow. I have one candid thought. Perhaps you could make the ending shorter. The ideas are good, but the last part is long. I want to be tactful, because your work is good. There is always room for improvement. We can talk about areas to improve on every week. One small improvement is a shorter ending. Please tell me what you think. I am glad to work with you. Best, Priya
lessons.sound: Tactful has its strongest beat on TACT. In tactful, say FUL clearly at the end. In candid, say CAN clearly at the start.
lessons.model: A tactful manager gives bad news kindly.
lessons.wordTask: What does Priya suggest to Daniel?
lessons.wordSample: She suggests he make the ending shorter.

lessons.title: Write a short performance review
lessons.goal: I can write a short performance review.

newItems.definition: How well someone does their work.
newItems.example: Her performance this year has been excellent.

newItems.definition: To judge the quality or value of something.
newItems.example: We need to assess the results before we decide.

newItems.definition: To study something carefully and judge how good it is.
newItems.example: The teacher will evaluate our essays this week.

newItems.definition: The things you do well and the things you do not.
newItems.example: Every review looks at strengths and weaknesses.

newItems.definition: Used to give a short ending to what you said.
newItems.example: To sum up, the project went well.

mainWord.definition: How well someone does their work.
mainWord.example: Her performance this year has been excellent.

lessons.mainWordForms: Performance is a noun. Performance is how well someone does their work. Her performance this year has been excellent.
lessons.expression: To sum up, Daniel has done very good work.
lessons.use: Use this to give a short ending to a review.
lessons.expressionTask: Maya writes a review of Daniel's first month. How does she end it?
lessons.grammar: Passive voice for formal writing: is or are + past participle
lessons.pattern: Daniel's work is praised by the team.
lessons.task: Daniel's work is ___ by the team.
lessons.example: Daniel's work is praised by the team.
context: Maya writes a short performance review for Daniel.
To sum up, Daniel has done very good work.
dialogue: Maya: Priya, I am writing a performance review for Daniel. Can you help me assess his work?
Priya: Of course. I will evaluate his report and his presentation.
Maya: Good. What are his strengths and weaknesses?
Priya: His ideas are clear. His endings are too long.
Maya: Thank you. To sum up, Daniel has done very good work.
Priya: Yes. His performance this month has been excellent.
lessons.listening: On Monday, Maya writes a performance review for Daniel. She asks Priya to help her assess his work. Priya says she will evaluate his report and his presentation. Maya asks about his strengths and weaknesses. Priya says his ideas are clear, but his endings are too long. Maya says, 'To sum up, Daniel has done very good work.'
lessons.question: What does Maya write for Daniel?
lessons.reading: On Monday, Maya writes a performance review for Daniel. It is the end of his first month at work. First, she asks Priya to help her assess his work. Priya says she will evaluate his report and his presentation. They sit together and talk about his strengths and weaknesses. His ideas are clear, and his first parts are strong. His endings are too long, but he listens well and he learns fast. Maya writes, 'Daniel has done very good work this month. His report is clear, and his presentation was excellent. He asks for feedback, and he uses it well.' To sum up, Daniel has done very good work. His performance this month has been excellent. Maya gives the review to Daniel. He reads it and says, 'Thank you, Maya. I am happy. I will work on my endings next month.'
lessons.readingQ: What does Maya write in Daniel's review?
lessons.readingA: She writes that his work has been very good and his performance this month has been excellent.
lessons.speaking: Tell a friend about a performance review you had. What did your manager say was good? What will you work on next?
lessons.speakingSample: Last month, my manager wrote a performance review for me. She asked my colleague to help her assess my work. My colleague said she would evaluate my report. They talked about my strengths and weaknesses. To sum up, I had done very good work. My performance that month had been excellent. I was happy, and I said I would work on my endings.
lessons.writing: Write a short performance review for a colleague. Say what they did well and what they can work on next.
lessons.writingSample: Performance Review: Daniel Lee. This month, Daniel has done very good work. His report is clear, and his presentation was excellent. He asks for feedback, and he uses it well. We talked about his strengths and weaknesses. His ideas are clear, and his first parts are strong. His endings are too long, but he listens well and he learns fast. To sum up, Daniel has done very good work. His performance this month has been excellent. Next month, he will work on short endings. Maya Chen, Team Lead
lessons.sound: Performance has its strongest beat on FOR. In performance, say MANCE clearly at the end. In assess, say SESS clearly at the end.
lessons.model: Her performance this year has been excellent.
lessons.wordTask: What does Maya write for Daniel?
lessons.wordSample: She writes a performance review for his first month at work.

lessons.title: Discuss strengths and areas to improve
lessons.goal: I can discuss strengths and areas to improve.

newItems.definition: Something you do well.
newItems.example: One of my strengths is explaining ideas clearly.

newItems.definition: Something you do not do well, or a fault.
newItems.example: Public speaking is still a weakness for me.

newItems.definition: A way of looking at or thinking about something.
newItems.example: From her perspective, the plan was too risky.

newItems.definition: In the way I see it.
newItems.example: From my perspective, the problem is the schedule.

newItems.definition: A new way of looking at something.
newItems.example: A new colleague can bring a fresh perspective.

mainWord.example: One of my strengths is explaining ideas clearly.

lessons.mainWordForms: Strength is a noun. The plural is strengths. A strength is something you do well. One of my strengths is explaining ideas clearly.
lessons.expression: From my perspective, clear ideas are your strength.
lessons.use: Use this to share your view of someone's work.
lessons.expressionTask: Maya talks to Daniel about his work. What does she say from her perspective?
lessons.pattern: My first part is clearer than my ending.
lessons.task: My first part is ___ than my ending.
lessons.example: My first part is clearer than my ending.
context: Maya talks to Daniel about his strengths and areas to improve.
From my perspective, clear ideas are your strength.
dialogue: Maya: Daniel, let us talk about your strengths and areas to improve.
Daniel: Good. I want to know what I do well and what I can do better.
Maya: From my perspective, clear ideas are your strength. Your first part is clearer than your ending.
Daniel: Thank you. What is my weakness?
Maya: Your weakness is long endings. But you listen well, and you learn fast.
Daniel: A fresh perspective helps me a lot. I will make my endings shorter.
lessons.listening: On Tuesday, Maya talks to Daniel about his work. She says, 'Let us talk about your strengths and areas to improve on.' Daniel says he wants to know what he does well. Maya says, 'From my perspective, clear ideas are your strength.' Daniel asks about his weakness. Maya says his weakness is long endings. Daniel says a fresh perspective helps him a lot.
lessons.question: What does Maya say is Daniel's strength?
lessons.reading: On Tuesday, Maya talks to Daniel about his work. She says, 'Let us talk about your strengths and areas to improve on.' Daniel says, 'Good. I want to know what I do well and what I can do better.' Maya says, 'From my perspective, clear ideas are your strength. Your first part is clearer than your ending.' Daniel says, 'Thank you. What is my weakness?' Maya says, 'Your weakness is long endings. But you listen well, and you learn fast. A fresh perspective helps us all.
